back: Embedding lookup → N blocks (norm, attention with KV cache, residual add, norm, MLP, residual add) → final norm → LM head → logits → sampler → next token.
Unnormalised scores, one per vocabulary token (32,000 for Llama 2), produced by the LM head from the last position's residual.

front: Where are most of Llama 2 7B's parameters?
back: In the MLPs: 3 × 4,096 × 11,008 ≈ 135 M per layer vs 67 M for attention. About two thirds of the total.

front: FLOPs per token for a dense model?
back: ≈ 2 × parameters (one multiply and one add per weight), plus an attention term ≈ 4 × layers × context × hidden size.
FLOPs performed per byte moved to or from memory. Compare it with the GPU's ridge point to see which limit binds.
Peak FLOP/s ÷ memory bandwidth. With 1,000 TFLOP/s and 3.35 TB/s (assumed): ≈ 300 FLOPs per byte.

front: Intensity of fp16 weight matmuls processing T tokens per pass?
back: ≈ T FLOPs per byte: 2T FLOPs per weight ÷ 2 bytes per weight. Tokens per pass is the intensity.
All prompt tokens share one pass, so intensity ≈ prompt length (thousands), well above the ridge of a few hundred.

front: Minimum decode step time at batch 1?
back: Weight bytes ÷ memory bandwidth. Llama 2 7B fp16: 13.5 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 4 ms, so at most about 240 tokens/s.

front: Why doesn't batch 64 give 64× decode throughput?
back: Batching amortises weight reads but every sequence's KV cache is still read each step. At 1k contexts it was 71% of bytes moved, giving about 19×.
p(i) = exp(zᵢ / T) ÷ Σ exp(zⱼ / T). Low T sharpens, high T flattens; T → 0 is greedy argmax.
Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability sums to at least p, so its size adapts to the model's confidence.

front: What does a seed fix, and what not?
back: It fixes the random draw. It does not fix the logits: if numerics shift upstream, the same seed can pick a different token.
A kernel gives bit-identical results for a row whatever the batch size. Most fast kernels lack it because they change reduction strategy with shape.

front: Main cause of temperature-0 drift on shared endpoints (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025)?
back: Batch size varies with server load, and kernels' reduction order depends on batch size, so floating-point rounding changes and near-tied tokens flip.

front: Why does MoE amplify numerical noise?
back: A tiny change in router scores can flip a near-tied expert choice, sending the token through entirely different weights; capacity caps also make routing depend on the batch.
